disclaimer: General educational summaries for a project prototype. Not medical advice. Cross-check against the ICMR/MoHFW guideline corpus before displaying to users.

diseases.name: Malaria (P. vivax / P. falciparum)
diseases.transmission: Bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito
diseases.summary: A parasitic infection of red blood cells causing fever with chills and rigors, headache and body ache. P. falciparum can progress quickly to severe disease (cerebral malaria, severe anaemia, organ failure). P. vivax is usually milder but can relapse weeks to months later because of dormant liver stages.
preventive_methods: Sleep under insecticide-treated bed nets
Indoor residual spraying in endemic areas
Use mosquito repellents, screens and long-sleeved clothing, especially at dusk and night
Eliminate stagnant water where Anopheles breed (larval source management)
Get tested early when fever occurs in endemic areas and complete the full course of treatment
Doctor-advised chemoprophylaxis for travellers to high-risk areas

diseases.name: Dengue (including dengue haemorrhagic fever)
diseases.transmission: Bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes (mainly Aedes aegypti), which bite in the daytime
diseases.summary: A viral fever with high temperature, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain and rash. A minority progress to severe dengue (plasma leakage, bleeding, shock), usually around the time the fever settles. A later infection with a different serotype carries higher risk of severe disease.
preventive_methods: Remove or cover water-holding containers (coolers, tyres, buckets, plant trays); empty and scrub weekly
Use repellents, long clothing and window/door screens during the day
Community vector control (fogging, larvicide) run by local health authorities
Seek care early if warning signs appear (persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, bleeding)
Vaccines exist in some countries with eligibility restrictions; check current availability and recommendations locally

diseases.name: Typhoid (enteric) fever
diseases.causative_agent: Salmonella Typhi (and Salmonella Paratyphi A for paratyphoid)
diseases.transmission: Faecal-oral route through contaminated food and water
diseases.summary: A systemic bacterial infection causing prolonged, gradually rising fever, headache, abdominal discomfort, and constipation or diarrhoea. Untreated, it can cause complications such as intestinal bleeding or perforation. Some recovered people become long-term carriers.
preventive_methods: Drink safe (boiled, filtered or treated) water and avoid ice of unknown source
Wash hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet
Eat freshly cooked food; avoid raw or street food of doubtful hygiene
Improve sanitation and safe sewage disposal
Typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV) for at-risk groups per national guidance

diseases.name: Scrub typhus / Murine typhus
diseases.causative_agent: Orientia tsutsugamushi (scrub typhus); Rickettsia typhi (murine typhus)
diseases.transmission: Scrub typhus: bite of infected chigger (larval mite) larvae. Murine typhus: infected rat fleas
diseases.summary: Rickettsial fevers causing fever, headache, myalgia and sometimes rash. Scrub typhus may show a black scab-like eschar at the bite site (not present in all patients) and can progress to pneumonia, meningoencephalitis or multi-organ failure if untreated. Both respond to appropriate antibiotics when started early.
preventive_methods: Avoid or limit contact with scrub vegetation and grassy or bushy areas; do not sit directly on the ground there
Wear long sleeves and trousers tucked into socks; use repellents (permethrin-treated clothing where available)
Wash and dry clothes and bathe after outdoor exposure
Rodent control and keeping surroundings clean (murine typhus)
Flea control on pets and in homes
No licensed vaccine is available

diseases.name: Leptospirosis
diseases.transmission: Contact of broken skin or mucous membranes with water, soil or mud contaminated by urine of infected animals (rats, cattle, dogs, etc.); outbreaks often follow floods
diseases.summary: A bacterial zoonosis ranging from a flu-like illness with fever, myalgia and conjunctival redness to severe disease (Weil's disease) with jaundice, kidney failure and bleeding, including lung haemorrhage.
preventive_methods: Avoid wading or swimming in floodwater or stagnant water
Wear boots and gloves in high-risk work (farming, sewage, animal handling) and cover cuts
Rodent control and safe food and waste storage
Wash and disinfect after exposure; use safe drinking water
Doctor-advised antibiotic prophylaxis for selected high-risk exposures

diseases.name: Chikungunya
diseases.transmission: Bite of infected Aedes aegypti or Aedes albopictus mosquitoes
diseases.summary: A viral fever with abrupt high temperature and severe, often symmetrical joint pain, plus rash and headache. The joint pain can persist for weeks to months in some patients. Deaths are uncommon, but it can be severe in newborns, older adults and people with other illnesses.
preventive_methods: Same vector control as dengue: remove standing water, cover containers, use screens
Repellents and protective clothing, especially during the day
Protect infected people from further mosquito bites during the first week of illness to avoid onward spread
Vaccines have been licensed in some countries; availability and safety guidance have been evolving, so verify the current status

diseases.name: Viral influenza-like illness (ILI)
diseases.causative_agent: Influenza viruses and other respiratory viruses
diseases.transmission: Respiratory droplets and aerosols, and contact with contaminated surfaces
diseases.summary: An acute respiratory viral illness with fever, cough, sore throat, body aches and fatigue. Usually self-limiting, but can become severe in older adults, young children, pregnant women and people with chronic conditions.
preventive_methods: Annual influenza vaccination, particularly for high-risk groups
Frequent handwashing and cough/sneeze etiquette
Stay home when ill; wear a mask around others and in crowded or high-risk settings
Good ventilation of indoor spaces
Avoid close contact with people who have flu-like symptoms

diseases.name: Hepatitis A / Hepatitis E
diseases.causative_agent: Hepatitis A virus (HAV) and Hepatitis E virus (HEV)
diseases.transmission: Faecal-oral route, mainly via contaminated water and food
diseases.summary: Acute viral liver infections causing fever, fatigue, nausea, loss of appetite, dark urine and jaundice. They are generally self-limiting and do not become chronic in healthy people. HEV can be particularly dangerous in pregnancy.
preventive_methods: Drink safe water and eat properly washed or cooked food
Handwashing with soap after toilet use and before handling food
Improved sanitation and safe sewage disposal
Hepatitis A vaccine is available and recommended in many settings
HEV vaccine access is limited to a few countries; check current availability

diseases.name: Occult bacteremia (pneumonia / UTI-pyelonephritis / intra-abdominal source)
diseases.causative_agent: Various bacteria (for example Streptococcus pneumoniae, E. coli and other Gram-negatives)
diseases.transmission: Not a single disease: bacteria enter the bloodstream from a primary focus such as the lungs, urinary tract or abdomen, and the source may not be obvious at first
diseases.summary: A bloodstream bacterial infection that presents as fever with few localising signs. The cluster entry groups hidden-source infections such as pneumonia, UTI/pyelonephritis and intra-abdominal infection. Delay in recognition can lead to sepsis.
preventive_methods: Keep vaccinations up to date (pneumococcal, Hib and others per schedule)
Treat urinary, respiratory and abdominal infections early and completely
Maintain hydration and good catheter and wound care
Seek prompt medical evaluation for persistent fever without a clear cause
Manage underlying conditions such as diabetes

diseases.name: Acute rheumatic fever
diseases.causative_agent: Immune reaction following Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) throat infection
diseases.transmission: Not directly contagious: it follows untreated or inadequately treated strep pharyngitis, which spreads by respiratory droplets
diseases.summary: An autoimmune inflammatory disease occurring typically 2 to 4 weeks after strep throat, mainly in children and young people. It can affect the heart, joints, brain (chorea) and skin, and repeated episodes can cause permanent rheumatic heart disease.
preventive_methods: Primary prevention: timely diagnosis and full antibiotic treatment (usually penicillin) of strep sore throat
Secondary prevention: long-term penicillin prophylaxis (commonly benzathine penicillin injections) after an episode
Reduce overcrowding and improve housing and hygiene
Regular follow-up and cardiac screening for people with a history

diseases.name: Tuberculosis (prolonged fever presentation)
diseases.transmission: Airborne, through droplet nuclei from people with active pulmonary TB
diseases.summary: A chronic bacterial infection that most often affects the lungs but can involve any organ. It typically presents with fever lasting more than two to three weeks, cough, weight loss and night sweats. Curable with a full course of anti-TB therapy; incomplete treatment risks drug resistance.
preventive_methods: Early diagnosis and complete treatment of active cases to cut transmission
BCG vaccination in infancy (protects mainly against severe childhood forms)
Good ventilation, cough etiquette and masks near infectious patients
Contact tracing and TB preventive treatment for eligible contacts
Address risk factors such as undernutrition, HIV, diabetes, smoking and alcohol use
